papers.title: Programmable Dissipation via Partial Quantum Error Correction
papers.abstract: Noise is typically treated as the adversary of quantum information processing. For open quantum dynamics, however, dissipation is part of the target physics, creating a tension with fault-tolerant architectures designed to suppress decoherence. Here we show that logical noise can instead be turned into a calibrated resource. We treat the error-correction cycle as a programmable primitive: one fault-tolerant round induces a logical completely positive trace-preserving map, and decoder/recovery randomization generates a controllable family of logical channels whose convex mixtures realize Kraus-channel mixing. This enables direct compilation of target dissipators into effective logical dynamics without explicit ancilla qubits for encoding the bath degree of freedoms. We derive an accuracy criterion for multi-step simulation in which the code distance is chosen so that uncontrolled logical errors remain a small fraction of the intended dissipation per step, rather than being driven below an arbitrarily small closed-system tolerance. Partial quantum error correction thus repurposes fault-tolerant structure to sculpt dissipation, offering a resource-efficient route to quantum simulation of open quantum systems.

summary.summary: This work shows that quantum error correction (QEC) cycles can be repurposed to programmably synthesize target dissipative dynamics at the logical level by treating the syndrome-averaged channel as a CPTP map and randomizing recovery operations. The framework enables resource-efficient simulation of open quantum systems on fault-tolerant devices through convex mixtures of implementable logical channels, avoiding explicit bath registers needed by dilation-based approaches.
summary.motivation: Fault-tolerant quantum computing architectures suppress all noise, but simulating real open quantum systems requires controlled dissipation as part of the target physics. Standard approaches embed dissipative channels into unitary evolution via Stinespring dilations, consuming $O(n)$ additional logical qubits for bath degrees of freedom; partial QEC instead converts calibrated noise into a programmable resource.
summary.method: One QEC round (syndrome extraction, decoding, conditional recovery with discarded classical records) generates a CPTP logical channel $\mathcal{B}_d = \mathcal{D}_d \circ \mathcal{Q}_d \circ \mathcal{C}_d$. Randomizing the recovery operation or decoder over a library $\{\mathcal{G}_k\}$ produces convex mixtures $\mathcal{G}_r = \sum_k r_k \mathcal{G}_k$ that span Kraus channels. Target dissipators are compiled by solving a convex optimization problem in logical Choi space using Frank-Wolfe, with complexity scaling as $\mathcal{O}(LM^2(d)/\eta)$ in library size $M(d)$ rather than physical Hilbert-space dimension.
summary.result: For two-site exciton dynamics with dephasing and amplitude damping ($\gamma_j$, $\gamma_{12}$, $\kappa_j$ rates), Strategy A (model-aware, using calibrated physical noise) and Strategy B (post-correction programming) both achieve trace distance $\lesssim 1\%$ from exact Lindblad evolution. Strategy A reduces code distance by setting it to uncontrolled errors only (Eq. 20: $\epsilon_\mathrm{un}(d) + \epsilon_\mathrm{prog}^A + \nu_d \lesssim \zeta \Delta_\mathrm{tar}(\tau)$), yielding qubit overhead scaling as $[d(x_B)/d(x_A)]^2$ with target-aware threshold $x_A = \zeta \Delta_\mathrm{tar}(\tau) \gg \epsilon/m = x_B$; Strategy B avoids model-calibration sensitivity and eliminates bath ancillas.

papers.title: Non-Clifford Crosstalk Noise in Surface Codes Using Hybrid Stabilizer-Tensor Network Methods
papers.abstract: Scalable realisation of quantum computing is reliant on the development of fault tolerant devices. Analysis of quantum error correction protocols typically considers incoherent noise models or noise-free syndrome measurements. While this is simple to simulate classically and straightforward to compute analytically, these simplifications are unable to capture the full dynamics of a noisy quantum system. In this work we use advanced hybrid stabilizer-tensor network simulation techniques to simulate coherent quantum crosstalk noise during syndrome extraction on a surface code. We show that the inclusion of coherence increases logical error rates and lowers the code threshold. In addition, we show that the specific distribution of the noise can quantitatively change logical error rates. The methods in this work allow simulation of quantum error correction with noise models previously inaccessible to classical simulation, providing new insights on the effect of crosstalk noise on quantum error correction codes.

summary.summary: This work uses hybrid stabilizer-tensor network methods to simulate coherent crosstalk noise during syndrome extraction in surface codes, capturing non-Clifford noise dynamics inaccessible to previous classical simulations. The inclusion of coherence in the noise model increases logical error rates and lowers the code threshold compared to incoherent-only models.
summary.motivation: Standard surface code analyses assume incoherent noise or perfect syndrome measurements, missing the coherent crosstalk that arises during multi-qubit syndrome extraction in realistic devices.
summary.method: Hybrid stabilizer-tensor network simulation techniques are used to model coherent quantum crosstalk noise during the syndrome extraction process in surface codes, allowing classical simulation of previously intractable non-Clifford noise.
summary.result: Coherent noise increases logical error rates and reduces the threshold for fault-tolerant operation; the spatial distribution of crosstalk noise quantitatively affects performance metrics.
